description: The future of humanity is inextricably linked to space, its exploration, and development. Even a small contribution from our team to this grand undertaking matters - that's our philosophy.
summary:
Humanity speaks of a future among the stars. Yet where in this future is the place for an ordinary person?
We created M.O.S.S. Simulation (Mission Operations & Space Science)—an educational game where the player leads a space research program. You select scientific goals, design spacecraft, choose instruments, manage limited resources, and launch missions. Your decisions shape the outcome: a powerful instrument demands energy, while detailed observations require reliable communications.
M.O.S.S. directly addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by weaving these choices into a complete mission lifecycle. Post-mission reports explain how spacecraft engineering and flight conditions impacted the results, allowing players to learn through their own experiments.
Just how important is this? Well, how important is air to a human being?
Our goal is to give players a sense of personal connection to humanity’s cosmic future. Before people can help build that future, they must first have the chance to think: “There is a place here for my decisions, too.” And if enough people think this way - and take even the smallest action - it could play a monumental role in the future of humankind
details:
A Place for Your Own Decisions

A school student might be able to list every planet in the Solar System, yet have no idea why a spacecraft needs one specific instrument over another. The distance between knowing facts about space and understanding a space mission cannot be measured in kilometers.

M.O.S.S. gives players the opportunity to bridge that gap.

Our project is an educational game about space mission design where the player leads a research program. You decide what to study, assemble the spacecraft, plan the mission, and analyze the consequences of your choices. We want curiosity to lead to action-and for those choices to become something a person can understand, question, and use to make the world even a little bit better.

How the Game Works

The journey begins with an interactive map of the Solar System. The player selects a destination and a scientific objective, determines an available flight profile, and plans the mission.

In the spacecraft builder, you choose scientific instruments and core subsystems: propulsion, power sources, batteries, onboard computers, attitude control systems, antennas, shielding, upper stages, and launch vehicles. Equipment options vary in mass, power consumption, cost, and suitability for specific tasks.

The mission forecast responds dynamically to these choices. A more advanced instrument can boost scientific output while simultaneously placing heavier demands on the entire spacecraft. Simply assembling a collection of expensive parts does not guarantee a successful mission.

Once a mission is complete, a postflight report breaks down the success score into individual contributions and explains the outcome. Players earn research points and progress toward the campaign goal of 100 Scientific Progress Points, freely choosing the sequence of their research.

Engineering Decisions with Clear Consequences

Imagine sending a remarkable camera across the Solar System, only to discover that your spacecraft cannot transmit enough of what it saw. You built a magnificent eye and barely gave it a voice.

This interdependence of components is at the heart of M.O.S.S. Players must consider what an instrument can measure, whether the spacecraft can sustain its operation, and if the gathered data can actually be sent back to Earth. Equipment yields scientific value only when it serves the chosen objective. An expensive particle detector does not become useful for imaging just because of its price tag.

The mission report reveals these dependencies. A failed outcome becomes a question worth investigating: Was it the wrong instrument? Did the craft run out of power? Did limited communications bottleneck the scientific data return?

Our Creative Approach

We wove the idea of personal agency into the very structure of the game. The player sets priorities, allocates resources, and takes ownership of the outcome. Their progress is built entirely on their own decisions

A transparent scoring system helps players make sense of complex trade-offs. Instrument specializations and component compromises encourage experimentation with different designs. The final report gives players a clear reason to rethink their strategy and try again

During development, we sought a balance between technical depth and accessibility. We accounted for scientific goals, hardware suitability, mass, power, communications, budget, mission duration, and clear feedback. Certain parameters and coefficients were intentionally simplified to keep gameplay engaging. M.O.S.S. is an educational model-its scores evaluate in-game performance rather than serving as a certified reliability forecast for real-world missions

Development

Built using JavaScript, we developed the project through iterative prototyping, testing and refining mechanics powered by real physics equations- such as the conservation of momentum and circular orbital dynamics.

The Impact We Aim to Achieve

Our audience consists of space enthusiasts who rarely get the chance to view an entire space mission as a single interconnected system.

We want players to walk away from the game asking questions they wouldn't have known how to ask before: What is worth exploring? What is the true cost of a more precise measurement? What else on the spacecraft has to change if I upgrade just one component? And how will this change the world?

We hope that for some, the impact will reach beyond the scren-sparking the realization that there is room for their curiosity, their decision-making, and their future work in the exploration of space.
